Listen to this article Share Synafare, a renewable energy supply-chain and financing company, is targeting 100 solar merchants with financing of up to N100 million each through a digital trade platform designed to improve equipment procurement, expand distribution and help businesses reach new markets. The initiative combines financing with access to manufacturers, authorised distributors and logistics services, as the company seeks to address working-capital and supply-chain constraints facing Nigeria’s solar energy businesses. Tobi Esho, chief executive officer and co-founder of Synafare, announced the initiative at the company’s Solar Roundtable 2.0 in Lagos on Saturday, October 24. He said the company, established about two years ago, had expanded beyond providing credit to solar installers to connecting businesses across the renewable energy supply chain. Read also: Europe prepares for historic total solar eclipse as Nigeria awaits 2027 “ring of fire” Synafare said it currently works with more than 2,000 businesses in the sector, providing supply-chain support and financing to help them purchase equipment and execute projects. Its platform covers inverters, batteries, solar equipment, energy-efficient appliances, electric bikes and tricycles. Through relationships with manufacturers and authorised distributors, the company offers logistics and buy-now-pay-later financing to installers, end customers and distributors seeking to purchase products, including in bulk. The model combines digital trade infrastructure with access to credit, enabling participating businesses to procure equipment without necessarily paying the full purchase cost upfront. It also seeks to help merchants secure competitive prices and diversify their income by moving beyond installation services into equipment retail and distribution. “Credit doesn’t go to businesses just because they exist. Financial institutions want to see predictability, structure and business activity,” Esho said. Under the new initiative, individual merchants can access financing of up to N100 million, depending on their turnover, with a typical minimum financing amount of about N10 million. Esho disclosed that two merchants had received a combined N170 million before the event officially began. For the roundtable, Synafare negotiated special prices with participating distributors and reduced its monthly financing rate from the usual four to five per cent to 3.5 percent. The financing push comes as solar businesses seek to serve households, commercial customers and communities with limited or unreliable electricity access. However, the ability to secure equipment and credit does not automatically translate into sustainable growth, particularly where businesses lack skilled workers, quality controls and the capacity to execute larger contracts. Babafemi Isaac, founder and chief executive officer of Kommercial Solar Limited, said his business had grown from residential installations to serving larger customers, requiring a bigger workforce and training for roofers and other artisans while maintaining quality standards. Chinwe Udo Udun Davies, founder and chief executive officer of Instoller, highlighted the importance of staff training and digital tools in enabling solar businesses to expand across multiple locations. “The cost of not training your people means your business can go down,” she said, urging business owners to invest in employee development rather than attempt to manage every aspect of their operations themselves. Tega Ishaya, a COREN-registered electrical engineer and commercial development associate at Elektron Energy Development Strategies Limited, said Nigeria’s electricity access gap presented opportunities for solar companies serving both underserved consumers with unreliable electricity and unserved communities without electricity access. She urged businesses to develop solutions for both markets, highlighting the commercial opportunities available to companies able to match customer needs with appropriate energy systems. For Synafare, expanding access to financing and equipment is central to helping merchants capture these opportunities. Its strategy also reflects a broader role for technology-enabled trade platforms in connecting suppliers, financing and last-mile businesses in Nigeria’s renewable energy market. The initiative’s progress will depend on the number of merchants financed, their ability to manage borrowing costs and whether access to equipment and working capital translates into higher sales, improved margins and expanded solar installations. She currently covers the Technology and Health beats for BusinessDay newspaper, where she writes in-depth stories on digital innovation, telecom infrastructure, healthcare systems, and public health policies.
